headline: S&P sets a new record on cooler headline PPI — but the core-core ran hot, and two more ADNOC tankers were hit overnight
client_frame:
Two stories worth separating. **The S&P 500 set a genuine new all-time high Thursday**, closing **7,798.99** — above the prior record close of 7,757.64 from August 7 — with an intraday high of 7,816.70 that also cleared the August 5 peak of 7,793.68. Both verified against daily history. To be precise about scope: **this is an S&P record only.** The Nasdaq 100 reclaimed 30,000 at 30,084.50 but sits **1.88% below** its June 2 peak, and the Dow is **0.94% below** its August 5 high. September hike odds fell to **hold 65.9% / hike 34.1%**, the third straight decline from 49.6% hike on Monday.

The reason for the rally was headline PPI at **0.0% MoM** against +0.2% expected, with the YoY rate dropping to 4.7% from 5.5%. But the print was two-sided, and the part that matters for policy went the other way: **core ex-food, energy and trade services rose +0.4% MoM, up from +0.1% in June.** Driving it was a **5.6–6.5% monthly surge in portfolio management services prices** — which is worth sitting with, because those prices largely track asset values. The market rally is mechanically feeding measured inflation. Pantheon lifted its July core PCE estimate to **+0.24% from +0.16%**, attributing roughly **11bp to that single component**, and expects the BEA's **September 30 methodology revision** to subtract at least 0.2pp from core PCE year-over-year. So the near-term data looks firmer than the headline while a scheduled statistical change points the other way. Neither is really about underlying inflation.

Meanwhile the long end kept telling a different story than stocks. Thursday's **$25B 30-year auction cleared at 5.216%, the highest in over 15 years**, with bid-to-cover slipping to 2.39x from 2.44x and primary dealers absorbing 11.5% versus a 10.6% average. Coupled with Wednesday's 10-year at a post-2007 high yield, that is two consecutive auctions of softening demand — real deterioration, though neither produced a large tail. And overnight the **UAE accused Iran of attacking two ADNOC tankers** in Hormuz, ADNOC's 15th and 16th vessels struck since February, sending Brent back up 1.7%. Monday is the reported expiry of the 60-day negotiating window.

geo_headlines: **Two more ADNOC tankers attacked overnight** in Hormuz, per UAE accusations against Iran — no injuries, situation 'brought under control', but ADNOC now counts 15 vessels struck since February and the UAE Foreign Ministry called it 'piracy' by the IRGC.

**Oil reversed hard on the news:** Brent +1.7% to **$88.51** and WTI +1.9% to **$82.79** in early Friday trade, after Thursday settles of $86.92 and $81.25 that were down roughly 2.3% on demand-forecast cuts.

**Monday August 17 is the reported expiry** of the June interim MOU's 60-day negotiating window. An Anadolu report claims the US and Iran agreed in principle to extend it, but that is **uncorroborated** — Al Jazeera and CNN describe the MOU as fraying, and Iran's foreign ministry says there are no negotiations with Washington.

**30-year auction confirmed the long-end problem:** 5.216% high yield, highest in 15+ years, bid-to-cover 2.39x vs 2.44x prior, indirects ~66.8%, dealers took 11.5% vs a 10.6% average. Tail only 0.4bp on the when-issued basis.
**Jobless claims 209,000**, above consensus — the labor side keeps softening after July payrolls came in at -23,000.
**Fed speakers split Thursday:** Hammack stayed hawkish while Barkin was more balanced. The dollar slipped back below 100 on DXY but Hammack's remarks limited the decline.
**Gold gave back its CPI gains** — $4,356.43, down 1.31%, after touching $4,449.37 intraday. A clear outside-day reversal.
**Canada's 50% Section 338 tariffs** on ~$20B of goods still take effect 12:01am ET **Wednesday August 19**, with no deal confirmed.
**The IEA raised its Q3 Brent forecast** to roughly $85 average, $11 above its July projection, while still expecting ~$78 by Q4 and ~$69 by Q1 2027 as traffic normalizes.
